warmup.q: The shop search runs on three machines. Its index is split into 3 pieces, and each piece has one copy on a different machine from the original. One machine is switched off. What does a search for every shop return a few seconds later?
options: About two thirds of the shops: the stopped machine's pieces are gone
Every shop, because each piece still has a copy on a running machine
An error until the machine comes back
Every shop, but only after the cluster has copied the missing pieces
warmup.why: The stopped machine held one copy each of two pieces, called shards, and each of those shards has its other copy on a running machine. The node in charge of the map promotes a copy wherever a shard's main copy went missing, so every shard still has a main copy and every document is searchable. The cluster reports its health as yellow. Building new copies comes later, after a one-minute wait, and only restores the spare copies, so the last option is the trap. Losing data needs both copies of a shard to go.

sections.h: When one machine is too small: split the index into shards, and copy each one
sections.html:
Let's start where Indexes for text, time and vectors left off. There, OpenSearch, a free search program built on the Lucene code library, kept the shops' names in an inverted index. That's a list, for every word, of the documents that contain it. (A document is one thing you can search for, here one shop.) It ran on one machine, a node in OpenSearch's words. The index had one piece and no copies: number_of_shards: 1, number_of_replicas: 0. For a dozen shops, that's right.

Now put the notes on disputed payments behind it, the cases where a customer says a charge was wrong. That's 30 million documents and about 120 GB of index, growing every month. Three things go wrong. The index keeps pushing against one machine's disk and memory. Every search runs on the one node, so its processors cap the searches per second. And when the node restarts for an update, search is down until it's back.

Version 1 is a bigger machine. It buys time for the first two problems, does nothing for the third, and gets expensive fast.

Version 2 splits the index, like the encyclopedia split into volumes. OpenSearch divides an index into a fixed number of primary shards, and each shard is a complete Lucene index, with its own lists of documents for every word. The shards spread over the nodes, so three nodes hold a third each and search in parallel. Each document lives in exactly one shard. OpenSearch picks it with a hash, a number worked out from the document's routing value, which is its id, _id, unless you say otherwise:

shard = hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards

% is the remainder after dividing, and it's why the number of primaries is fixed when you create the index. Change 3 to 4 and almost every remainder changes, so most documents belong in another shard. Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys measured hash mod S, the same remainder, moving 80% of the keys. OpenSearch won't move documents for you. You create a new index and copy every document into it, called reindexing, or _split the index into a multiple of its shard count, 3 into 6.

The split works because the formula is a shorthand. For a 3-shard index, OpenSearch really hashes into 768 routing slots and gives each shard 256 slots in a row. Splitting 3 into 6 cuts each shard's slots in two, so every document lands in one half of its old shard. The lab checks this against the real cluster. The encyclopedia picture breaks here: its volumes are cut by letter and can be cut again at any time, while OpenSearch's cut comes from a hash fixed at creation.

Version 3 copies each shard. A replica is a full copy of a primary on another node, kept up to date on every write. If a node dies, the replica still has the data. It serves searches too, so more replicas mean more searches a second. The one placement rule: a replica never sits on the same node as its primary or another copy of its shard. A photocopy on the same shelf as the original protects nothing. Unlike primaries, you can change number_of_replicas at any time. An index created with no settings gets 1 primary and 1 replica.

An index is a fixed number of primary shards, each with replicas on other nodes. Choose the number before the data arrives. Something must keep the map of which copy lives where. Next, we'll meet the node that does.

sections.h: One elected node, the cluster manager, keeps the map
sections.html:
Ask any node of the lab cluster for _cat/shards and you get the same table. Every node knows it, but only one may change it. The table is part of the cluster state. That's the list of nodes, every index's settings and mappings, and the routing table, which says which copy of which shard lives on which node. (Mappings describe each field, such as which ones hold text.) Each node keeps a copy of the cluster state and routes requests with it.

One node, the elected cluster manager, is the only one that changes it. That's OpenSearch's answer to the question Rebalancing and request routing asked: who holds the map? The manager decides where new shards go, notices when a node disappears, and sends every new version of the state to all the nodes. In the library, it's the head librarian, who keeps the catalogue of which shelf holds what.

A node's roles say what it may do, and you set them with node.roles:

Role What the node does
cluster_manager may be elected cluster manager (it's "eligible"), and votes in elections
data holds shards: adds documents to them and runs searches on them
ingest runs ingest pipelines, steps that reshape documents before they're stored
coordinating every node: takes a client's request, sends it to the right shards and merges the answers

A node with node.roles: [] does only the last job. The lab's three nodes are all cluster_manager and data. A big cluster usually runs three small nodes that only manage, and separate data nodes. Then a data node that pauses to clean up its memory (Java's garbage collection) can't hold up changes to the cluster state.

How do the eligible nodes agree on one manager? By voting. A candidate becomes manager when a majority of the voting nodes vote for it. Every election starts a new term, a number that goes up by one each time, as in Raft, which the Consensus track builds. The manager checks every node once a second and removes one that misses three checks in a row. The other nodes check the manager the same way, and start an election when it goes quiet.

Majority is why you need three eligible nodes. With two, a majority is two. If either fails, the other can't win an election, and nothing that needs the manager can happen: no new indexes, no promoted replicas, no shards placed. With three, any two carry on. Majority also prevents split brain, two managers each running part of the cluster. A network failure can leave at most one side with a majority, so two managers never accept conflicting changes.

Two settings start all this. discovery.seed_hosts lists the addresses where a starting node looks for the others. cluster.initial_cluster_manager_nodes names the eligible nodes that may vote in the very first election, and it's read only once, when the cluster forms for the first time. Next, we'll use the map: a write goes to one place, and a search goes everywhere.

sections.h: A write goes to the primary, a search to one copy of every shard
sections.html:
Send a new shop, PUT merchants/_doc/M-0054, to any node, and that node coordinates the request. It hashes M-0054 (shard 2), looks up shard 2's primary in its cluster state, and forwards the request there. The primary adds the document to a buffer in memory and appends the operation to its translog, a write-ahead log on disk. The translog is forced onto the disk (fsync) before the write is confirmed (index.translog.durability: request), so a crash can't lose it.

Then the primary sends the operation to every in-sync replica, each copy of the shard that's up to date. It sends to all of them at once, and waits for each one to do the same. Only then does the client get its answer, which says "_shards": {"total": 2, "successful": 2}: both copies have it. The primary gives every operation a sequence number. It also stamps a primary term, which goes up each time a replica is promoted, so replicas can tell old operations from new ones.

Confirmed doesn't mean searchable yet, because the buffer isn't part of the inverted index. Every second (index.refresh_interval: 1s), each shard copy turns its buffer into a new Lucene segment, a small inverted index of its own that never changes, and opens it for searching. That refresh is why OpenSearch is called near-real-time: a document shows up in searches up to a second after the write returns. A GET by id doesn't wait for it, and finds the latest version at once. Since segments never change, a delete is a mark and an update is a new version. In the background, merges combine small segments into bigger ones, like the compaction in LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters. A flush is a Lucene commit, a saved point that lists every finished segment: it forces the segments onto the disk and trims the translog.

A search fans out, and Secondary indexes across shards said why. A shard's inverted index covers only that shard's documents, like the index at the back of one volume. No shard can say which other shards hold matches, so the coordinator has to ask them all. It sends the query to one copy of every shard, primary or replica, picking the copy that has answered fastest lately (adaptive replica selection).

That's the query phase. Each shard scores its own documents with BM25, the ranking formula from Indexes for text, time and vectors. It returns only the ids and scores of its best from + size. (size is how many hits a page shows, and from is how many to skip.) The coordinator merges those lists into the overall top. Then it runs the fetch phase: it asks for the full documents of the page it will return, and nothing else. So from: 9990, size: 10 on 5 shards makes every shard find its top 10,000, and the coordinator sorts 50,000 hits to return 10. That's why index.max_result_window stops from + size at 10,000 by default; to page deeper, use search_after, which carries on from the last hit of the page before.

And a search is as slow as its slowest shard. Say each shard answers within some time limit 99% of the time. Then all 10 shards of a search do so only 0.99 to the power 10, about 90%, of the time.

A search asks every shard. More shards add work to every search.

Fanning out has one more effect. Each shard works out BM25's idf, how rare a word is, from its own documents only. With millions of documents per shard, the shards agree and nobody notices. With a few documents they don't, and the ranking can change, which the Try-it shows. search_type=dfs_query_then_fetch adds a first round trip that collects those numbers from every shard. Next, we'll switch a node off and watch the map change.

sections.h: When a node leaves: promote a replica, wait, copy, and turn green again
sections.html:
Cluster health sums up the whole routing table in one colour. Green: every primary and every replica has a node. Yellow: every primary has a node, but at least one replica doesn't. All the data is there and searchable, with fewer copies than you asked for. Red: at least one primary has no node, so some documents can't be searched, and writes to that shard fail.

Let's watch what a node failure does to the map, because every step is a decision the cluster manager makes. The manager notices first: the node misses three checks a second apart, and the manager removes it from the cluster state. For each primary the node held, the manager promotes an in-sync replica on another node. That's instant, because the replica already has every confirmed write, and the shard's primary term goes up by one. Every copy the node held is now missing, so each becomes an unassigned replica, a copy with no node, and health turns yellow.

Then the manager waits. Copying a shard means reading every segment from the primary and writing it to another node, and if the node was only restarting for an update, that work is wasted. So for one minute (index.unassigned.node_left.delayed_timeout), the unassigned replicas stay unassigned, in case the node comes back with its copies intact.

After the minute, the manager gives each missing replica a node that holds no copy of that shard, preferring nodes with fewer shards. The new copy pulls the primary's segments, which is called a peer recovery. It's limited to 40 MB a second per node by default (indices.recovery.max_bytes_per_sec), so a 30 GB shard takes about 13 minutes. When every copy has started again, health is green, now on fewer nodes. When the node returns, or a new one joins, the balancer moves copies onto it until each node holds about the same number. (The balancer is the part of the manager that evens out the nodes.)

Red needs every copy of a shard gone at once. With one replica, that's the two nodes holding a shard's two copies failing before a new copy is built. A brand-new empty node can't fix it. Only the lost node coming back with its disk, or a restore from a snapshot (a backup of the index's files), brings that shard back. Two replicas make it a three-node failure, at the price of a third copy of every byte. In the library, red is both shelves that held one volume collapsing together.

The stepper walks through each decision. Next, we'll decide how big each shard should be, and set up the nodes.

try.title: Take a node away and watch yellow turn green
steps: Look at the shard table, then stop a node other than os1 that holds a primary. The awk line, a small tool that picks fields out of text, chooses it; sparing os1 keeps port 9200 answering.
Read the health, the shard table and the document count straight away. Predict which copies are unassigned, and whether the count is still 13.

Wait for green (about a minute; the health call waits for you), then read the table and the recoveries. Bring the node back with docker compose -f env/opensearch-cluster.yml up -d --wait, give the balancer a minute, and see where the copies are.

sections.h: How big a shard should be, and how to set up the nodes
sections.html:
We know how the pieces behave; now let's size them. OpenSearch's documentation says to keep shards between 10 and 50 GB, and both limits have reasons. A 200 GB shard is slow to move: at 40 MB a second, its peer recovery takes well over an hour, while the shard has one copy fewer. And one shard's search can't spread over more nodes. Thousands of 100 MB shards fail differently. Every shard is a Lucene index with its own files, its own memory and its own entry in the cluster state, and every search pays one request per shard. cluster.max_shards_per_node stops you at 1,000 shard copies per node by default.

So pick the number of primaries from the size you expect: 120 GB of disputes at about 30 GB a shard is 4 primaries. For data that grows for ever, such as logs, create one index per day or week and roll over to a new one when the time comes. Shard sizes then stay put, and old data leaves by deleting whole indexes.

Each node's settings live in a file, config/opensearch.yml. The essentials for a three-node cluster:

cluster.name: sfz-search            # nodes join only a cluster with the same name
node.name: os1
node.roles: [cluster_manager, data]
network.host: 0.0.0.0               # bind to a real interface, not just localhost
discovery.seed_hosts: [os1, os2, os3]
cluster.initial_cluster_manager_nodes: [os1, os2, os3]   # first start only
path.data: /var/lib/opensearch

The heap is the memory the node's Java program may use, set in config/jvm.options or OPENSEARCH_JAVA_OPTS. Make the starting size, -Xms, equal to the maximum, -Xmx. Use half the machine's memory, and no more than about 31 GB, so that Java keeps its compressed object pointers, a trick that makes references between objects smaller.

The other half isn't wasted. Lucene reads most of its segment files through memory-mapped files, which Copy-on-write, mmap and the OOM killer showed in the Operating systems track. So the operating system's page cache, its copy of recently read file data in memory, holds the busy segments, and a search served from it never touches the disk. Lucene maps many files, which is why Linux needs vm.max_map_count of at least 262,144. A node that listens on a real network address, not only inside its own machine, enforces that and other startup checks, and refuses to start if one fails. Turn swap off, so the operating system never moves the heap out to disk. And watch the disk: at 85% full a node gets no new shards, at 90% the manager moves shards away, and at 95% the indexes on that node become read-only.

The lab switches off the security plugin to keep curl simple, so it runs plain HTTP, with no encryption between nodes and no users. Never do that outside a laptop. A real cluster needs TLS, the encryption behind https, for clients and between nodes, plus users and roles.

Elasticsearch, the program OpenSearch came from, works the same way, and the lab runs OpenSearch 3.9.0. OpenSearch began in 2021 as a fork, an independent copy, of Elasticsearch 7.10.2, so shards, replicas, routing, refresh and the cluster manager carry over (Elasticsearch still calls it "master"). The difference is the licence, the terms on which you may use and change the code. OpenSearch is under Apache 2.0, while Elasticsearch ships under the Elastic License 2.0, with an AGPLv3 option added in 2024. The Try-it reads these limits from the running cluster.

refs.title: OpenSearch documentation: installing OpenSearch, important settings

opening:
Picture an encyclopedia in three volumes, each with its own index at the back. To find every page that mentions bicycles, you open all three indexes and put the pages together. No volume can tell you what the others hold. Now picture a librarian who keeps a photocopy of every volume, on a different shelf from the original. A shelf collapses, and nothing is lost.

The support team's shop search works the same way. The search index grew too big for one machine, so it was split over three. Switch one machine off, and it's easy to expect a third of the shops to vanish, because a third of the data lived there. They don't, and the reason is where the copies sit.

DynamoDB under the hood found every item by its key, on one partition. A search for a word has no key to follow. In this lesson, we'll split a search index over three machines, follow a write and a search, and switch a machine off. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with an encyclopedia whose volumes each had their own index, with photocopies on other shelves. OpenSearch works the same way: every search reads every shard's index, and one machine switched off loses nothing, because each shard keeps a copy elsewhere.

Next time a site's search says "page 1 of 1,000", try jumping to the last page. Many sites won't let you, and now you know why: every shard would have to rank everything before it.

That ends the Partitioning track, where each write changed one document. Next, the Transactions track asks what happens when one payment must change several records together, while other payments change them too.

The cluster node names its roles, the seed hosts where it finds the others, and the eligible nodes that vote in the first election. It listens on a real network address, so the startup checks are enforced. The lab's Compose files set these as environment variables, and both turn off the security plugin, which only a laptop should do. cluster.name must match on every node of a cluster.

lab.title: Model a search cluster: routing, placement, failover, health and query then fetch
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. One test passes (the given routing hash), and nine fail.

Write shardFor, two lines from the KDoc (the comment above it). One test checks it against the shards the three-node cluster chose for M-0042 to M-0054, and another splits 3 shards into 6 and checks that no document changes halves.
Write health, then allocate: replicas only, never next to a copy of their own shard, fewest copies first. Three tests check the exact placements on one, two and three nodes.

Write nodeLeft: take the node's copies away and promote a replica for each lost primary, without placing anything. Two tests replay the stepper: yellow, then green on two nodes after allocate, then red when two nodes go before any copy is rebuilt.
Write ShardedIndex.search: ask every shard for its top from + size, merge, keep the page and fetch only that. The deep-page test counts the hits the shards send back. All ten pass.
hints: shardFor: val slots = routingNumShards(primaries), then Math.floorMod(routingHash(routing), slots) / (slots / primaries). Kotlin's % keeps the sign of a negative hash; floorMod doesn't.

allocate: for each unassigned replica, val start = nodes.indexOf(primaryNode), scan (1..nodes.size).map { nodes[(start + it) % nodes.size] }, drop nodes that already hold a copy of the shard, then minByOrNull { copiesOn(it).size }, which keeps the first of equals.

nodeLeft: loop over copiesOn(node).sortedBy { it.shard }, a copy of the list, so you can change the copies. For a lost primary, find copiesOf(shard).firstOrNull { !it.primary && it.node != null }, set its primary = true, and set the lost copy's primary = false.
search: compareByDescending<Hit> { it.score }.thenBy { it.id } is the order everywhere. Each shard's list is take(from + size), and the page is drop(from).take(size) of the merged list.

drill.title: A node failure, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking: an index has 3 primaries and 1 replica on nodes A, B and C, laid out as A: p0, r2; B: p1, r0; C: p2, r1. (a) Node B dies. Write the layout and the health just after the manager reacts, and again a minute and a recovery later. (b) Which two nodes would have to die together to turn the index red, and why? (c) Write the routing formula, and say why the number of primaries can't change.

answer.html:
(a) right after: shard 1's replica on C is promoted
      A: p0, r2     C: p2, p1     unassigned: r0, r1     -> yellow
    after the 1-minute delay and peer recovery (never next to its own primary):
      A: p0, r2, r1 C: p2, p1, r0                        -> green
(b) any two whose loss takes both copies of one shard: A and C (shard 2),
    B and C (shard 1), or A and B (shard 0), before a new copy is built.
    With 3 primaries and 1 replica on 3 nodes, any two nodes do it.
(c) shard = hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards, _routing = _id by default
    change the divisor and most documents belong to another shard;
    reindex into a new index, or _split into a multiple of the shard count

recap: An index is a fixed number of primary shards, each a whole Lucene index. A document goes to hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards (really 768 slots for 3 shards), so the number of primaries is set at creation; reindex or _split to change it.

Replicas are full copies on other nodes, never next to their own primary. They survive node failures and serve searches, and their number can change at any time. An index with no settings gets 1 primary and 1 replica.

Only the elected cluster manager changes the cluster state: the nodes, the index settings and the routing table. The eligible nodes elect it by majority, so run three; discovery.seed_hosts finds the others, and cluster.initial_cluster_manager_nodes starts the first election.

A write goes to the primary (a buffer plus the translog), then to every in-sync replica before it's confirmed, and a refresh every second makes it searchable. A search asks one copy of every shard for its top from + size, merges the lists and fetches only the page.
When a node leaves, replicas are promoted, missing copies wait a minute, and peer recovery rebuilds them: yellow, then green. Red means every copy of some shard is gone.

The limit: every search asks every shard, so more shards add work to each search, and the number of primaries can't change in place. Keep shards at 10 to 50 GB, the heap at half the memory and under about 31 GB, and security on for anything but a laptop.

explain.prompt: Your team is about to run a three-node OpenSearch cluster for dispute search. Explain to a colleague how a document is stored and found across the nodes, what happens when one node dies, and the three settings decisions you'd make on day one.
explain.answer: The disputes index is split into a fixed number of primary shards, each a full Lucene index, and every primary has a replica on a different node. A dispute goes to the shard picked by hashing its id and taking the remainder after dividing by the number of primaries. That's why the number is fixed when we create the index: changing it means reindexing. One node is the elected cluster manager. It keeps the map of which shard copy lives where, and every node routes with that map. A write lands on the shard's primary, goes into its buffer and translog, is copied to the replica, and only then is confirmed; it becomes searchable at the next refresh, within a second. A search goes to one copy of every shard, each returns its best ids and scores, and the node we asked merges them and fetches only the page we show. If a node dies, the manager promotes the replicas of the primaries it had. Health goes yellow, but every dispute is still searchable, and after a minute the manager rebuilds the missing replicas on the other nodes and we're green again. Red would mean both copies of some shard are gone. On day one I'd choose the number of primaries from the expected size, so shards stay between 10 and 50 GB. I'd keep one replica and make all three nodes eligible as manager, so any two can elect one. And I'd give each node a heap of at most 31 GB, leave the rest of the memory to the page cache, and switch security on.

deeper.html:
The most common sizing mistake is choosing the shard count by habit: Elasticsearch's old default of 5 primaries, or one index a day at whatever size that gives. It works at first, because small shards are fast. A year later the cluster has 9,000 shards of 200 MB, the cluster state is huge, every search sends hundreds of shard requests, and nodes hit cluster.max_shards_per_node. Or the opposite: one 400 GB shard that takes hours to recover after every restart. It happens because the primary count must be chosen before there's any data to measure. Estimate the size first, aim for 10 to 50 GB per shard, roll over data that grows for ever, and shrink or reindex old indexes that ended up with too many tiny shards.

Document replication, where every copy indexes every document, is the default (index.replication.type: DOCUMENT), and it means each replica spends as much processor time as its primary. OpenSearch also offers segment replication: only the primary indexes, and replicas copy its finished segments after each refresh. Indexing gets faster, and replicas lag the primary by a refresh or so. OpenSearch also has search replicas, on nodes with the search role: copies that only serve searches, so heavy indexing and heavy searching stop competing for the same nodes.

Shard allocation awareness spreads copies over places that fail separately. Give each node an attribute such as node.attr.zone: eu-west-1a and set cluster.routing.allocation.awareness.attributes: zone. The manager then puts a shard's primary and replica in different zones, so losing a whole zone leaves a copy of everything. The lab's same-shard rule is the one-zone version of this.

A replica is not a backup. A bad mapping change, a script that deletes the wrong documents, or a red index after a double failure all reach every copy or none. Snapshots are the backup: PUT _snapshot/<repo>/<name> copies the segment files to a repository such as S3, Amazon's file storage, and only the new files each time, because segments never change once written.

Sequence numbers make recovery cheap. Every operation on a shard gets a sequence number, and every copy tracks the highest one below which it has everything, its local checkpoint. When a node comes back within the delay, its replica needs only the operations above its checkpoint, which the primary keeps for it (a retention lease), instead of every segment again. The primary term in the Try-it's write response is the other half: after a promotion, operations from the old primary carry the old term and are rejected.

Elasticsearch shares all of this up to the 7.10 fork and has gone its own way since. In Elasticsearch 8 and 9 the defaults and some names differ (it never renamed "master"), and serverless Elasticsearch separates indexing and search onto different machines, with the data in cloud file storage. The routing formula, replicas, refresh and query then fetch are the same in both.
